title: Testing your own code
lesson:
Every exercise so far, Archie's tests told you whether your code worked. Real programs have no Archie. Professionals write **tests**: small pieces of code that call your code and check the answer. Then, every time you change something, you run them all in a second and know you didn't break anything.

**Why it matters for you:** a game has hundreds of rules (damage, armor, prices, spawns). Change the armor formula and maybe the boss becomes unkillable. You won't notice by playing for five minutes. A test notices instantly.

A test is three steps, often called **Arrange, Act, Assert**:

```
var w = new Wallet();            // arrange: set things up
w.Earn(5);                       // act: do the one thing
Check.Equal(5, w.Coins, "earn"); // assert: was the result right?
```

The `Check.Equal` helper throws a `TestFailedException` with a clear message ("earn: expected 5, got 0") when the answer is wrong. A **runner** calls every test, catches the failures, and prints a summary like `3 passed, 1 failed: overspend`. In real projects you'd use a test framework (xUnit or NUnit, and Unity has its Test Runner), but they do exactly this: you'll build a small one yourself so nothing is magic.

**What to test.** Not just the happy path:
- one **normal** case (30 damage, 10 armor gives 20);
- the **edges**: 0, exactly equal, one more than the limit, empty lists;
- **bad input**: negative numbers, null, and that the right exception is thrown;
- every **rule** in the spec gets at least one check.

**How to tell your tests are any good?** Break the code on purpose and see if a test fails. If you can change `Math.Max(1, ...)` to `Math.Max(0, ...)` and every test still passes, your tests don't really check that rule. Professionals call this **mutation testing**, and Archie's hidden tests in this unit do exactly that to *your* tests: they hand your checks some broken versions of the code and expect your checks to catch every one.

**Common mistakes:**
- Tests that never fail (checking `x == x`, or catching every exception).
- One giant test that checks twenty things: when it fails you don't know which.
- Only testing the case you just wrote the code for.

Delegates make tests flexible: a test method that takes a `Func<int, int, int>` can check *any* damage formula, the real one or a broken one. That's the trick this unit uses.

notes: Check.Equal works for any type T and throws with a clear message.
Each test is an Action (a small function with no result) stored under its name.
The runner catches failures so one failing test doesn't stop the others.
The 'no hit' test fails: Damage(0, 5) gives 1. The test found a real bug in the formula.

exercises.title: A Check helper
exercises.prompt:
TestFailedException is given. In static class Check write:
- Equal<T>(T expected, T actual, string what): if they differ (use EqualityComparer<T>.Default), throw TestFailedException("{what}: expected {expected}, got {actual}").
- True(bool condition, string what): if false, throw TestFailedException("{what}: expected true").
- Throws<TException>(Action action, string what) where TException : Exception: runs action. Passes if it throws a TException. If it throws something else: "{what}: expected {TException name}, got {other name}". If nothing is thrown: "{what}: expected {TException name}, nothing was thrown". (Names like ArgumentException: typeof(TException).Name.)

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { try { Check.Equal(4, 2 + 2, "sum"); return "passed"; } catch (TestFailedException e) { return e.Message; } }))()
tests.name: equal passes

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { try { Check.Equal("maize", "beans", "crop"); return "passed"; } catch (TestFailedException e) { return e.Message; } }))()
tests.name: equal fails clearly

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { try { Check.True(5 > 9, "big"); return "passed"; } catch (TestFailedException e) { return e.Message; } }))()
tests.name: true fails

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { try { Check.Throws<ArgumentException>(() => throw new ArgumentException(), "guard"); return "passed"; } catch (TestFailedException e) { return e.Message; } }))()
tests.name: throws passes

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { try { Check.Throws<ArgumentException>(() => { }, "guard"); return "passed"; } catch (TestFailedException e) { return e.Message; } }))()
tests.expect: guard: expected ArgumentException, nothing was thrown
tests.name: nothing thrown

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { try { Check.Throws<ArgumentException>(() => throw new InvalidOperationException(), "guard"); return "passed"; } catch (TestFailedException e) { return e.Message; } }))()
tests.name: wrong exception

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { try { Check.Equal<string>(null, null, "nulls"); return "passed"; } catch (TestFailedException e) { return e.Message; } }))()
tests.name: null equals null
tests.hint_if_fail: expected.Equals(actual) crashes on null: use EqualityComparer<T>.Default.Equals(expected, actual).

hints: Equal: if (!EqualityComparer<T>.Default.Equals(expected, actual)) throw new TestFailedException($"{what}: expected {expected}, got {actual}");
Throws: try { action(); } catch (TException) { return; } catch (Exception e) { throw new TestFailedException(...e.GetType().Name...); }
After the try/catch (nothing was thrown), throw the 'nothing was thrown' failure.

exercises.title: Tests that catch bugs
exercises.prompt:
The armor rules: Damage(raw, armor)
  1. raw of 0 or less does 0 damage.
  2. negative armor counts as 0.
  3. otherwise the damage is raw - armor, but always at least 1.
Write ArmorMath.Damage(int raw, int armor) to follow them. Then write ArmorTests.AllPass(Func<int, int, int> damage): run your own checks on the function you are GIVEN and return true only if it follows every rule. Archie will hand it your Damage (must give true) and several broken versions (each must give false). Cover a normal case and every rule's edge.

tests.call: ArmorTests.AllPass((r, a) => r <= 0 ? 0 : Math.Max(1, r - a)).ToString()
tests.name: catches: negative armor not handled
tests.hint_if_fail: Add a check with negative armor, e.g. (10, -5) should be 10.

tests.call: ArmorTests.AllPass((r, a) => Math.Max(1, r - Math.Max(0, a))).ToString()
tests.name: catches: zero raw still hurts
tests.hint_if_fail: Add a check that raw 0 gives 0.

tests.call: ArmorTests.AllPass((r, a) => r <= 0 ? 0 : Math.Max(0, r - Math.Max(0, a))).ToString()
tests.name: catches: minimum of 0 instead of 1
tests.hint_if_fail: Add a check where the armor is bigger than the hit: it should still do 1.

tests.call: ArmorTests.AllPass((r, a) => r <= 0 ? 0 : Math.Max(1, r - Math.Max(0, a) / 2)).ToString()
tests.name: catches: armor only half counted
tests.hint_if_fail: Add a plain normal case, like (30, 10) gives 20.

hints: Damage: if (raw <= 0) return 0; armor = Math.Max(0, armor); return Math.Max(1, raw - armor);
foreach (var c in cases) if (damage(c.Raw, c.Armor) != c.Expected) return false; return true;

exercises.title: A tiny test runner
exercises.prompt:
1. TestRunner.Run(Dictionary<string, Action> tests): run every test in order. A test fails if it throws (any exception); a failure must not stop the others. Return "{passed} passed, {failed} failed", and if any failed add ": " and the failed names in order, joined by ", ".
2. WalletTests.All(): return at least 3 named tests for the given Wallet class (they must all pass on it). Cover earning, overspending, and that Earn(0) throws.

tests.call: TestRunner.Run(new Dictionary<string, Action> { ["a"] = () => { }, ["b"] = () => throw new Exception("boom"), ["c"] = () => { }, ["d"] = () => throw new InvalidOperationException() })
tests.name: failures are listed

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var t = WalletTests.All(); return (t.Count >= 3) + " " + TestRunner.Run(t).StartsWith(t.Count + " passed, 0 failed"); }))()
tests.name: your wallet tests pass

hints: foreach (var (name, test) in tests) { try { test(); } catch (Exception) { failed.Add(name); } }
string summary = $"{tests.Count - failed.Count} passed, {failed.Count} failed"; add ": " + string.Join(", ", failed) when there are failures.
A wallet test: ["earning adds coins"] = () => { var w = new Wallet(); w.Earn(5); if (w.Coins != 5) throw new Exception("expected 5"); }

quiz.q: What are the three steps of a typical test?
quiz.why: Set up, do one thing, check the result.

quiz.q: Your Damage tests all still pass after you change Math.Max(1, ...) to Math.Max(0, ...). What does that tell you?
choices: No test checks the 'at least 1' rule: add one
quiz.why: That's the idea behind mutation testing.

quiz.q: Which is the best set of cases for 'armor reduces damage, minimum 1'?
quiz.why: A normal case plus every edge.

quiz.q: Why should a runner catch each test's exception separately?
choices: So one failing test doesn't stop the rest from running

quiz.q: What's wrong with a test that wraps everything in catch (Exception) { }?
choices: It can never fail, so it checks nothing
quiz.why: A test that can't fail isn't a test.

cards.a: Set up, do one thing, check the result

cards.q: What makes a good set of tests?
cards.a: A normal case, the edges (0, equal, limit, empty) and bad input
Break the code on purpose; a good test suite notices
